quote: Kann man immer Zahlen so adjun- giren, dass jene [-Ge-] Teilbarkeitsgesetze gelten?
english: Can one always adjoin numbers in such a way that those divisibility laws hold?
topic: The page covers systems (number domains) closed under operations, with examples from ring and field theory, questions on when divisibility laws hold in integral domains, and a plan for teaching function theory by combining Weierstrass with Riemann–Cauchy.

triage.modern_statement: Given the ring of integers O_K of an algebraic number field K, where unique factorization into primes can fail (Kummer, Dedekind), can one always adjoin further algebraic numbers, i.e. pass to a finite extension L/K, so that the divisibility laws hold? There are two standard readings. (a) Weak version: does every ideal of O_K become principal in O_L for some finite extension L, so that Kummer's 'ideal numbers' turn into actual numbers? (b) Strong version: is there a finite extension L with class number 1, meaning O_L is a UFD? This is the class field tower problem.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert himself conjectured (1898) that the Hilbert class field H(K) does (a). This is the principal ideal theorem, proved by Furtwängler around 1930, building on Artin's reduction to group theory. Under reading (b) the answer is no in general: in 1964 Golod and Shafarevich found number fields (e.g. Q(√-3·5·7·11·13·17·19)) whose class field tower is infinite, so no finite extension of them has class number 1.

evidence.claim: The principal ideal theorem, which Hilbert conjectured in 1898, says every ideal of a number field K becomes principal when extended to the Hilbert class field of K. The proof is attributed to Artin and Furtwängler.
Principal ideal theorem of class field theory: extending ideals maps the class group of K to the class group of its Hilbert class field (it becomes trivial).
In 1964 Golod and Shafarevich showed that certain quadratic fields, e.g. Q(√-3·5·7·11·13·17·19), have an infinite 2-class field tower.
The class field tower question asks whether K lies in a finite extension L with class number 1. Golod–Shafarevich (1964) gave a negative answer.
Kummer kept unique factorization for cyclotomic integers by introducing 'ideal numbers', which later became the modern notion of ideals.

triage.why: The note's wording ('adjoin numbers so that those divisibility laws hold') matches the classical question of realizing Kummer's ideal numbers inside a larger number field. I'm inferring that reading from the context: the page discusses integral domains and when divisibility laws hold. The note is short, so which version Hilbert meant can't be confirmed. If he meant the weak version (make every ideal of K principal), the answer is yes: the Hilbert class field does it, by the principal ideal theorem that Hilbert conjectured and Artin and Furtwängler proved around 1930. If he meant the strong version (full unique factorization in some finite extension), the answer is no, by Golod–Shafarevich 1964. Either way the question has been answered, and it is not one of the 23 problems. Capitulation and class field towers are still active research topics: the arXiv papers cited here, which study principalization and infinite towers, date from 2014 to 2025.
